title: Thinking recursively
description: Recognize the pattern. Build the solution. Make it faster.

parts.title: Your starting point
parts.label: Pre-test
parts.description: A short, unassisted check of what you already know. This is a baseline, not a lesson grade.
parts.question: Complete the four diagnostic questions without assistance.

parts.title: A smaller version of the same problem
parts.label: Discover
parts.description: Open the nesting dolls, watch the calls build up, then follow the returns back out.
parts.question: Explain what the smallest solid doll represents, and why each recursive step must make progress toward it.
parts.theory: Recursion solves a problem using smaller instances of the same problem. A base case is handled directly without another recursive call. A recursive case reduces the input and uses the smaller result. Calls wait on a stack until their subproblems return. In the Russian nesting doll analogy, opening a doll reveals a smaller similar doll; the smallest solid doll is the base case. Then results return outward, one waiting call at a time. Use this analogy conversationally and ask one brief check-in question at a time.

parts.title: Choose, build, and trace
parts.label: Build & trace
parts.description: Choose a problem with self-similar subproblems, write Fibonacci recursively, and trace fib(4).
parts.question: Which of the three problems naturally has branching self-similar subproblems? Implement fib(n) with fib(0) = 0 and fib(1) = 1. State the recurrence and trace fib(4), including its returned value and maximum stack depth.
parts.theory: The suitability choices are Fibonacci, scanning a list once to find a target, and Celsius-to-Fahrenheit conversion. Fibonacci has the natural branching recurrence fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2). A linear scan is usually simpler as a loop; a conversion is a direct formula. Recursion is a suitable structure, not a necessity: Fibonacci can also be implemented iteratively. For the standard naive fib(4) call tree there are nine calls, the result is 3, and the maximum stack depth is four frames when the root counts as one. Do not reveal these answers or write the learner's function; ask targeted questions about progress, termination, and combining smaller results.

parts.title: Remember the work you have already done
parts.label: Optimize
parts.description: Find repeated calls, then use a dictionary to avoid calculating the same subproblem again.
parts.question: Count the fib(2) calls in the naive fib(4) tree. Implement fib_memo(n) using a dictionary, checking cached results before expanding and storing new results before returning. Explain the change in time and space complexity.
parts.theory: Naive fib(4) calls fib(2) twice: one computation is redundant. Memoization reuses results keyed by the input. A cache lookup must precede expanding recursive branches; a new result must be stored before returning. Under constant-time dictionary access and unit-cost arithmetic, naive Fibonacci has exponential time (O(2^n) is a useful upper bound), while memoized Fibonacci has O(n) time, O(n) cache space, and O(n) stack depth. This is top-down dynamic programming. A bottom-up alternative computes results from base cases upward, which is only introduced here. Guide with small hints; do not provide complete code or the full answers.

parts.title: A new problem, on your own
parts.label: Transfer
parts.description: Apply what you learned to a new problem, without AI support, hints, or reference answers.
parts.question: There are n stairs. Each move climbs either one or two stairs. Count the distinct sequences of moves that reach the top. For n = 0 there is one way: take no moves. Write a recursive memoized function climb_stairs(n), then explain your base cases, recurrence, cache lookup/storage, and time complexity.

pretest.prompt: Which description best captures a self-similar subproblem?
options: A smaller problem with the same structure as the original
Any operation that runs faster on a computer
A problem that uses the same variable names
A problem that has no possible base case

pretest.prompt: A function repeatedly calls itself with n - 1. What else is needed to ensure it stops for non-negative integer inputs?
options: A base case that returns directly when the input is small enough
A loop around every recursive call
A new function name for every call

pretest.prompt: Given fib(0) = 0, fib(1) = 1, and fib(n) = fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2), what does fib(3) return?
A call tree contains the same subproblem with identical inputs more than once. What would memoization do?
options: Save the result and reuse it for the same input
Make a separate copy of the full input for every call

suitability.title: Fibonacci numbers
suitability.description: Find the nth number when each number is the sum of the two previous numbers. What smaller versions of this problem could you solve?

suitability.title: Find a target in a list
suitability.description: Check a flat, unsorted list from left to right until you find a target value. A single pass is enough.

suitability.title: Convert a temperature
suitability.description: Convert one Celsius value to Fahrenheit using a fixed arithmetic formula.
